author: haiku
reason: A shows the actual schema and the exact SQL for creating and checking sessions, puts the error paths in the flows, and gives a table of what fails and what the user sees, so a newcomer can see exactly how the system works; B is easier to read but leaves the tables as prose, keeps login errors out of its diagram, and has small inaccuracies such as a fixed Retry-After of 900 seconds.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with the system context A leaves out (a server-rendered app, two instances without sticky sessions, a shared Postgres, an unchanged users table), and it backs each choice with the actual schema and SQL statements, step-by-step flows, a failure table that includes error paths in the diagram, and a requirement-coverage map, so a newcomer can see exactly how the system behaves rather than only why each choice was made.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A starts by describing the system as it is today: a server-rendered app on two instances, the existing users table and bcrypt. It then defines every term (advisory lock, dummy hash, fail closed) and gives the full schema, numbered steps and a failure table. Document B assumes you already know the project, and its checklist refers to numbered requirements it never states.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for an outsider to follow: it describes the existing system first (server-rendered app, two instances, the users table), defines its terms, then covers the schema, each flow step by step, a storage-failure table, trade-offs and open questions; A assumes you already know the context and ends with a table that maps to numbered requirements the reader never sees.

author: haiku
reason: Document A describes the current system and the new runtime first: keys copied in constructors, the image deciding the read path, and how holder snapshots, readiness and refresh behave. It then gives a rollout that runs in order and explains why rollback stays safe. Document B's steps run out of numeric order (16 and 17 before 12, 15 before 14), and it leaves the runtime behaviour to the end, so a newcomer has a harder time building a working picture of the system.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it explains how the system works at runtime before the rollout steps, runs its steps in one straight order, and spells out mechanisms A only hints at (the image alone decides how a pod gets its keys, what happens to requests in flight, why a rollback works until revocation, who acts on each failure), while A makes the reader jump steps (16/17 before 12, 15 before 14) and says running pods would pick up a bad key at step 10, when no new-code pods exist yet.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a five-step overview of the whole migration and defines the terms an outsider needs, such as APP_ENV, maxUnavailable and old key/new key; it also explains why the design is safe (immutable old images keep their keys, and readiness gating protects the rolling deploy), so the system is easier to understand than in B, even though B has a nice failure table and a canary step.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives an outsider a clearer working model of the system: a start-to-finish flow, a list of rules that hold throughout, and the reasons behind the mechanics (how rolling deploys use readiness, why old pods still hold keys in their immutable images, why the old key waits until confirmation), while A is tidier but explains less about why things work.

author: haiku
reason: A gives a newcomer the more complete and internally consistent picture: today's system, its stated assumptions, full sequence diagrams, a token state machine, a dedicated worker section and a failure table. B is shorter but leaves gaps and contradictions, such as the worker invalidating links and raising alerts while the existing worker is described as notifying nobody.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover because it explains today's system and its own assumption (a Postgres queue), gives the reason behind each choice, and keeps one "live" test that the endpoints, the worker, a lifecycle diagram and a failure table all share; A is shorter but contradicts itself, saying the worker only logs and drops failed jobs, then later having it invalidate links and raise alerts without describing that change.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a one-screen map of the system, lays each flow out as short numbered steps and puts failures in a scannable table, so I would understand the system faster; A is more exhaustive, but its wide, busy diagram and long glossary make the core mechanism harder to pick out.

author: sonnet
reason: B is better for a newcomer: it opens with a plain overview, defines the terms a newcomer would not know (how sessions log devices out, what FOR UPDATE does, where the link points), notes that a failed enqueue leaves the user with no working link, and lists the open questions, while A is tighter and has the cleaner diagram but takes more of the project for granted.

author: haiku
reason: I'd rather be handed A because it stands on its own: it starts by summarising the existing password login, lockout and start_session, then walks through the diagram in numbered steps that explain why each check exists (for example, how the gflow cookie stops login CSRF). B sends the reader to existing/auth_flow.md for the current behaviour, and its flow-hash and cookie keying is harder to follow, even though its invariant section is useful.

author: haiku
reason: B is more self-contained for a newcomer: it opens with how the existing password login and sessions work, defines even basic pieces like Redis and Postgres, and walks through numbered steps in the same order as the diagram, explaining why each check exists (for example, login CSRF) and what start_session actually does; A sends the reader to outside files and explains the flow by topic rather than in sequence.
